summary: Describes a framework for sending only the changes to an XML document, rather than a full new copy. Each change is located using an XPath selector that points at the part of the document to add, replace, or remove. It gives other protocols a common way to express partial updates to XML data.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives a common way to describe changes to an XML file. Each change names the exact place it applies to with an XPath expression and says whether to add, replace or remove something there, so the sender can transmit the changes instead of the whole file.

questions: how to send only changes to an xml document
what is the xml patch framework
what does the sel attribute do in xml patch
subtitle: Sending the changes to an XML document instead of a whole new copy.

tldr.problem: To change an XML document over the network, the sender normally has to send a complete new copy of it, even when only one small part has changed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three patch operations, add, replace and remove, each with a sel attribute holding an XPath expression that names the one place in the document to change.
tldr.outcome: An application can send a document of just the changes, and the receiver applies them in order to arrive at the same result as a full copy would have produced.

today: RFC 5261 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it defines the patch elements that later formats, such as partial presence documents, build on.

sections.title: Why a Patch Format
sections.content:
XML documents are widely used as containers for the exchange and storage of arbitrary data in today's systems. In order to send changes to an XML document, an entire copy of the new version must be sent, unless there is a means of indicating only the portions that have changed.

This document describes an XML patch framework that uses XPath selectors. An XPath selector pinpoints the specific portion of the XML that is the target for the change. Those selector values and the updated data content are the basis of the patch operations described here. With the basic add, replace and remove directives, a set of patches can be applied to update an existing target document, which gives a simple semantics for data-oriented XML documents: additions, removals and substitutions of elements and attributes become easy to perform. The document is careful about its scope: it does not describe a full XML diff format, only basic patch operation elements that can be embedded within a full format that typically has additional semantics.

One concrete example given is a presence system built on SIP, where a partial PIDF XML document format combines the existing PIDF document format with the patch operation elements defined here. In general, patch operations can be used in any application that exchanges XML documents, for example within the SIP Events framework. Another example is XCAP-diff, which uses this framework to send partial updates of changes to XCAP resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing an XML file over a network usually means sending the whole file again. This RFC defines a smaller message: a list of changes, each naming the place it applies to. Other protocols, such as partial presence documents and XCAP updates, are built on top of it.

sections.title: The Words the Document Uses
sections.content:
The document defines the terms it needs. The target XML document is the document that is going to be updated with a set of patches. The XML diff document is the document that contains the patch operation elements, the namespace declarations and all the content changes needed to turn the target into a new document. The patched XML document is what results after the patch operations have been applied. A patch operation is a single change, and a patch operation element is the XML element that represents one.

A type definition for an element is a schema type definition that describes the content of a patch operation. In-scope namespace declaration means the list of namespace declarations in scope at a context node, the basis on which the qualified name of that node is expanded; for an element, one of those bindings may have an empty prefix. A positional constraint is a number in square brackets, usable as a location step predicate. A located target node is a node found in the target document with the help of an XPath selector value. A white space text node is a text node that contains only white space.
sections.plainLanguage: Three documents matter: the one being changed, the one carrying the changes, and the one that results. Each change is a single operation element, and it points at the node it applies to with a selector.

sections.title: What the Framework Covers
sections.content:
In this framework, the selector values and the new content are embedded in XML elements whose names specify the modification to be performed: add, replace or remove. These elements are defined by schema types, the selectors are expressed as attributes of those elements, and the child nodes of the patch operation elements hold the new data content. In general, and where it applies, the new content should be moved unaltered into the patched document.

XML documents that are equivalent for the purposes of many applications may differ in their physical representation, so the framework aims for determinism: the canonical form with comments of a document decides what counts as logical equivalence. White space text nodes therefore have to be processed properly, because white space is significant by default. The specifications that reference these schema types must define the full diff format with an appropriate MIME type and a character set such as UTF-8. As the schema in this document declares no target namespace, its type definitions inherit the target namespace of the schema that includes them, which avoids extra namespace declarations inside the diff documents.

The node types of the XPath 1.0 data model that can be added, replaced or removed are elements, attributes, namespaces, comments, texts and processing instructions. The full XML prolog cannot be patched, including XML entities and the root node of a document, although the comments and processing instructions of the root node can be patched. The root element itself cannot be removed or added, because a valid XML document must always have exactly one root element. Support for external entities is outside the scope of the framework.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework covers the parts of a document that carry meaning: elements, attributes, namespaces, comments, text and processing instructions. The XML declaration at the top of the file and the root element itself are off limits, because the file would stop being a valid XML document.

sections.title: How the Patches Are Applied
sections.content:
An XML diff document contains a collection of patch operation elements, including one or more add, replace and remove elements. These patch operations are applied sequentially in document order. After the first patch has been applied to update the target document, the patched document becomes a new independent document, and the next patch is applied to that one. The procedure repeats until all the patches have been processed successfully.

Each patch operation element carries a sel attribute whose value is an XPath selector drawn from a restricted subset of XPath 1.0. The value is used to locate a single unique target node in the target document. That node pinpoints the target for the change, and it is usually an element, which is either updated itself or has new child nodes added into it. It may also be, for instance, a comment node, after which other sibling nodes are inserted. In any case, it is an error condition if the evaluation of the selector finds multiple nodes.

The selectors always start from the root node of the document, so relative location paths should be used and the leading slash can be omitted. A node test can be the wildcard character or a qualified name; the wildcard selects all element children of the context node. Right after the node test, a location step can hold one or more predicates in any order. An attribute value comparison is one of the most typical predicates, and the string value of the current node or of a child element can be used instead. The character that denotes the current context node is an abbreviated form of the full XPath expression for it. Positional constraints such as [2] can be used as an additional predicate. The XPath id() function may also be used to identify unique elements, but then the schema describing the document must use an attribute of the ID type, or, with non-validating parsers, an xml:id attribute must have been used in the instance document.
sections.plainLanguage: The changes are applied one after another, each on the result of the last. Every change names exactly one place to work on, using a restricted form of XPath, and if the expression matches more than one place the change is an error.

sections.title: Matching Namespaces Across Two Documents
sections.content:
Namespace prefixes are normally local in scope, so a diff document may use different prefixes from the target document. The agent parsing the diff document must resolve prefixes separately in both documents in order to match the resulting qualified names. The diff document must contain declarations for all the namespaces it uses, and its own declarations are always what apply inside it.

A selector in a diff document may use prefixes when naming elements, and such a prefix must be looked up in the diff document's namespace declarations. If the patch operation element declares xmlns:a='foo:' and the selector is sel='a:bar', the agent must look for a bar element qualified with the foo: namespace, whatever prefix the target document uses for it.

Default namespaces make this harder to state. When the diff document has a default namespace declaration, an element selector without a prefix must be evaluated using that namespace. Unqualified names are possible too: if there is no default namespace declared and an element name appears without a prefix, it is an unqualified element name, and in a selector it must match an unqualified element in the target document, one with no prefix and no default namespace in scope.

These rules differ from XPath 1.0 and XPath 2.0. In XPath 1.0 a bar selector always locates an unqualified bar element, and in XPath 2.0 it also matches a qualified bar element in scope of a default namespace declaration. Here a selector without a prefix matches one element only, and it matches an element with or without a prefix only if the namespace it is qualified with, or none, is an exact match. The XPath functions namespace-uri() and local-name() may be used during evaluation but are not allowed by this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The two documents may name the same namespace with different prefixes, so the patch says which namespace it means, not which prefix. A name with no prefix means the diff document's default namespace, or a name with no namespace at all if there is no default namespace. This is stricter than XPath, and on purpose.

sections.title: The Three Operations
sections.content:
The add element represents the addition of new content to the target document, for example a new element appended into an existing one. The new content is the child nodes of the element, and when adding attributes and namespaces the child must be a single text node. It has three attributes: sel, type and pos. The type attribute is only used when adding attributes and namespaces, and then the located target must be an element into which they are inserted: a value of @attr means that the string after the at sign is the name of the attribute being added and the text of the element is its value, while a value of namespace::pref means that pref is the prefix of a new namespace declaration and the text is the namespace URI.

The pos attribute says where the new content goes. With neither type nor pos present, the children are appended as the last children of the located element. With pos of prepend they become the first children, with before they become the immediate preceding siblings of the located node, and with after the immediate following siblings. So <add sel="doc"><foo id="ert4773">This is a new child</foo></add> appends a foo element to the doc element, <add sel="doc/foo[@id='ert4773']" type="@user">Bob</add> adds a user attribute with the value Bob, and <add sel="doc" type="namespace::pref">urn:ns:xxx</add> adds a namespace declaration.

The replace element represents a replacement and always updates a single node or node content at a time. It has only the sel attribute. If the located node is an element, a comment or a processing instruction, the child of the replace element must be of the same type. Otherwise the element must have text content, and it may be empty when replacing an attribute value or text node content. Replacing an element removes all its descendants, namespace declarations and attributes; replacing an attribute value with an empty element leaves the attribute in place with an empty value; replacing a text node with an empty element removes the text node, since a text node must always have at least one character.

The remove element represents a removal and has two attributes, sel and ws. The ws attribute removes the white space text nodes that are immediate siblings of the located node, with the values before, after or both, and it may only be used when removing something other than a text node, an attribute or a namespace node.

White space needs care, because the XPath data model does not allow two text nodes to be immediate siblings. When an add operation brings a white space text node and the last child of the target is already a text node, the two are combined. The same applies when removing an element, a comment or a processing instruction that has text nodes on both sides without the ws directive: the contents of the two text nodes are combined and the second one disappears.
sections.plainLanguage: Add puts new content at a named place, replace swaps what is there for something new, and remove takes it away. Each says which place it means with a selector. The add operation also says where the new content should go, and the remove operation can take the surrounding spaces with it.

sections.title: When a Patch Cannot Be Applied
sections.content:
It is an error condition if any of the patch operations cannot be unambiguously fulfilled. Once a particular patch operation fails, processing of further patch operations is hardly sensible.

A new MIME error format is defined for applications that need deterministic error handling when a patch cannot be applied, and the error elements can be used inside other MIME types that allow extension elements. The root element of the error document is patch-ops-error, and its content is a specific error condition, with a different element for each condition so that different conditions can carry different data. All the error elements support a phrase attribute that can hold text meant for a human reader, and the optional xml:lang attribute may describe the language of that phrase. Most of the error elements are meant to contain the patch operation element that caused the failure.

The elements defined are invalid-attribute-value for content that is not allowed in the sel, type, ws or pos attributes or in an added attribute, invalid-character-set for a diff and a patched document using different character sets, invalid-diff-format for a body that is not well-formed XML or is not valid against its schema, invalid-entity-declaration for an entity reference that cannot be resolved, invalid-namespace-prefix for a prefix whose namespace URI cannot be located, invalid-namespace-uri for a namespace URI that is not valid or not declared in the target document, invalid-node-types for a replace whose content does not match the type of the located node or that has several nodes where one is needed, invalid-patch-directive for a directive that was not understood, invalid-root-element-operation for an attempt to remove the root element or add a sibling to it, invalid-xml-prolog-operation for failures on prolog nodes, invalid-whitespace-directive for a remove that asks for a white space node that is not there, unlocated-node when a single unique node cannot be located or when several are found, unsupported-id-function when the id() function is not supported, and unsupported-xml-id for the xml:id attribute. Additional error elements may be indicated inside the root element from any namespace, and the IETF may specify more in the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:patch-ops-error namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: If a change cannot be made exactly as asked, the whole operation fails and the rest of the changes are not attempted. The error is reported in a small XML document whose root element names the problem, such as the target node not being found, and it includes the change that caused the failure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations depend very much on the application that uses the framework. Each application has different needs, threat models and security features, so these have to be considered application by application.

There is one point that the document makes for all of them. This framework uses a limited subset of XPath 1.0, so applications may be vulnerable to XPath injection attacks that can reveal content of an XML document that the user was not allowed to see. Injection attacks are most likely with shareable resources, where a user's access to a resource is limited to specific parts of it, which is the opposite of the typical use of the framework. To defend against those attacks the input must be sanitized, which can be done, for example, by validating the diff formats against the restrictive schemas of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: What is safe depends on the application. The general warning is that the selector expressions come from somewhere, so a crafted selector could ask for parts of the document the sender was not meant to reach. The fix is to check the incoming changes against the restrictive schema before acting on them.

cells: Puts new content at the located place
Swaps the located node for new content of the same kind
Takes the located node away, optionally with the surrounding spaces

data.title: Three patch operations
data.code:
<add sel="doc"><foo id="ert4773">This is a new child</foo></add>

<replace sel="doc/foo[@a='1']"><bar a="2"/></replace>

<remove sel="doc/foo[@a='1']" ws="after"/>

viz.caption: HOW NAMES ARE MATCHED BETWEEN THE TWO DOCUMENTS

items.title: A prefixed name
items.text: The prefix is looked up in the diff document's own declarations.

items.title: A default namespace
items.text: A name with no prefix uses the diff document's default namespace, if it has one.

items.title: No prefix, no default
items.text: The selector then matches only an element with no namespace at all.

items.title: Added content
items.text: The target must end up with a declaration for the same namespace URI, whatever prefix it uses.

viz.caption: SOME OF THE ERROR CONDITIONS THE FRAMEWORK DEFINES

items.label: Unlocated node
items.desc: A single unique node could not be located, or several were found.

items.label: Invalid node types
items.desc: The replacement content does not match the type of the located node.

items.label: Invalid namespace prefix
items.desc: The namespace URI for a prefix could not be located or resolved.

items.label: Invalid diff format
items.desc: The body was not well-formed XML or not valid against its schema.

items.label: Invalid whitespace directive
items.desc: A remove asked for a white space node that is not in the document.

items.label: Invalid root element operation
items.desc: An attempt to remove the root element or add a sibling to it.

items.label: Unsupported id function
items.desc: The id() function is not supported, so attributes of the ID type are not known.
